His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available.

Implicit copulas are the primary choice for analyzing dependencies in complex scenarios due to their ability to effectively model dependence in high-dimensional spaces. The text presents a comprehensive overview of this broad category, encompassing copulas such as elliptical, skew t, factor, time series, and regression copulas, highlighting their key characteristics and applications. The discussion explains how the auxiliary representation of implicit copulas facilitates scalability and usability in statistical modeling, addressing concerns like parameter estimation, likelihood calculation, and model parsimony. The text also covers Bayesian estimation techniques for implicit copulas and the benefits of employing these models in conjunction with time series and regression models, which are the subject of current research advancements. The advantages of using implicit copulas are further illustrated through the examination of econometric applications, including analyses of macroeconomic time series and financial asset pricing.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in relation to the k-NN approach. An exact formula for the similarity score between two word vectors is derived, along with upper and lower bounds for the similarity scores. Additionally, this study investigates whether the similarity-based ranking of words aligns with their frequency within a given text corpus. Through a set of experiments, the stated formulas and bounds are validated, and the influence of various hyperparameters on the calculated similarity scores is assessed. The study reveals that the cosine similarity used in the marginalization process and the frequency-based distribution of words are key factors in the model's performance.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of type as a bi-module over this auxiliary space. This method allows our approach to draw from the established Lambek Calculus and its type-theoretic counterpart, while also drawing from the non-abelian fractional statistics and associated physics concepts to its semantic interpretation.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated strategies is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also compares these algorithms in practical game scenarios.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly focusing on scenarios where the epidemic is on the verge of spreading widely. In cases where the epidemic does not spread widely, proven results indicate that the model closely follows its theoretical equivalent. However, at the critical threshold for widespread spread, the model exhibits dramatic fluctuations and, in certain cases, leads to complete recovery of the network. Furthermore, the model's dynamics give way to simpler, well-studied stochastic processes, such as the M/M/1 queue, near this threshold.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes it easy to work with polynomial operators used in the quantum many-body theory by creating a specialized language for their manipulation. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive toolkit for the development of exact diagonalization codes, carefully designed for high performance, ease of use, and customization. libcommute boasts an intuitive syntax for commonly applied abstractions and algorithms, and its extensive documentation and comprehensive unit tests guarantee its stability. Furthermore, the Python 3 wrapper called pycommute provides a useful solution for smaller-scale diagonalization problems, quick prototyping, and the seamless integration of libcommute's performance-driven computational cores with Python applications.

Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for the assignment of both the smaller and larger gap values, consistent with band-folding theory. Our findings provide a comprehensive picture of the gap structure around the zone center in both superconducting and normal states.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints.

Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a phenomenon in which the intensity and phase of the reflected signal are interconnected, often disregarded in theoretical studies. By employing a statistical approach that examines the impact of adjusting the gain at each point on the reflecting surface, our team developed a sophisticated algorithm utilizing a technique known as coordinate descent to determine the optimal ANTECOR gain distribution. The key findings from our simulations reveal that taking into account the interdependence between phase and amplitude results in a significant decrease in system capacity, compared to theoretical models that do not consider this interdependence, thereby highlighting the importance of real-world considerations in designing efficient communication systems.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code is developed in C++ for maximum performance but also offers the flexibility to run on different systems using CMake. MG-GLAM supports creation of sophisticated simulations that include higher resolution multigrid structures, allowing researchers to customize and explore modified gravity simulations effectively.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under the assumption of conformal invariance. We relax this assumption and define Gaussian free fields on the set of domains within the complex plane that are invariant under rotation or reflection, along with the corresponding imaginary surface. Using this framework, we develop the Gaussian free field on the set of domains in the upper half-plane that are bounded below by the union of $N$ rays originating from $0$, denoted as ${\mathcal {D}}_{N}$, and introduce the Gaussian free field on ${\mathcal {D}}_{N}$ in a way that is consistent with the canonical process on the Dyson model ${\mathcal {M}}_{N}$, utilizing the explicit heat kernel discovered by Forr\'{e}s}.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame fluctuating in a linear acoustic vibration. However, existing linearization approaches that rely on the Reynolds-Oscillation decomposition neglect heat release fluctuations, which is a significant omission. To address this shortcoming, a new linearization framework has been developed which incorporates the effects of heat release fluctuations, which can be strongly influenced by flame noise and contribute to instability in flames. To validate the results obtained from this new approach, it was compared with both the outcomes of a fully compressible direct numerical simulation and previous predictions that ignored heat release fluctuations. The findings showed that including the effects of heat release fluctuations brought the predicted flame response into line with the results of the full simulation, while the earlier approach that ignored these effects resulted in an incorrectly predicted response and led to inaccurate predictions of flame response and instability.

We've discovered a hidden characteristic of stars, which originates from their topological nature, by drawing parallels between stellar behavior and the concept of topology applied to oscillations. To understand stellar dynamics, we compare the total energy of a star's vibrations to the gradient of changes made to its internal structure. This approach reveals that stars possess a topological framework, which can help make sense of complex stellar fluctuations. Our analysis focuses on two main aspects: the overall pattern of stellar vibrations and the impact of structural alterations on these vibrations. These concepts are explained using both mathematical formulas and visual representations of stars, which represent changes in their internal density. Ultimately, our findings connect to the study of stellar vibrations, and further research into this area is encouraged.

We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with nonlocal
randomly distributed coupling strengths.

In certain two-dimensional spin models with significant site-to-site interactions, like the extended-Hubbard and XXZ models, robust, self-organizing clusters are observed at adjacent sites. These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters interact with one another and their internal dynamics are set against each other. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers demonstrated that in a one-dimensional system, an alternative framework exists which incorporates this cluster-based interaction, akin to an XXZ spin model where magnetic interactions are modified by an intensity factor determined by the sum of inverse potentials. This new understanding enables the seamless transition from describing these interacting clusters to examining fermions within a lattice, as is often done in experimental settings. Furthermore, this paradigm shift yields distinct phase boundaries characterized by both stable, motionless clusters and fermionic liquid behavior, with possible signatures of hysteresis as a result. These findings are supported by numerical simulations and can be visually represented through spin correlations, as well as measured in cold atom experiments using inelastic scattering techniques.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 \nu \beta \beta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass would have difficulty detecting a signal.

The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons and limitations of existing methods to study them prompt research on new approaches. One such approach, called the "chameleon" method, allows for investigating these photons by observing their interactions with the Sun's magnetic field, which can cause ULHCOs, pair production, and proton dissociation. However, conventional methods are insufficient to study these photons using the chameleon approach. We propose a new, forward detection method capable of observing ULHCOs produced when ultra-high energy photons collide with the Sun's magnetic field. This method involves detecting electrons with energies above 100 TeV in a new direction of flight, which is 90 degrees from the incoming UV photons. We estimate the rate of these electrons to be between 1 and 10 per day, which can be studied with existing equipment like the HAWC and the upcoming HERD on the Tiangong-2 space station. This research was presented at the 33rd International Cosmic Ray Conference in 2019.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements based on associations with specific association signals, using a Bayesian framework. By estimating changes in allele-specific activity across elements, our method can be applied to various types of data sets. For example, enzyme-sensitive DNA sites related to blood type can be inferred from data sets that include blood type-related enzyme activity. Testing this model with 62,884 human genomes, we associated 748 genetic variations with blood type-related enzyme sensitivity in 10 different cell types. Furthermore, nearly 80% of these variations occur in elements showing altered activity in at least one cell type associated with blood type, which is a higher proportion compared to variations associated with other traits such as height or body mass index. Our approach can aid in blood type-related variant functional analysis by integrating existing data sets or via blood type-related models that consider linkage information. Moreover, this can be integrated into larger association analysis frameworks such as MANMAN to reduce false associations and increase statistical power based on biological context of traits or diseases.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, analysis based on maximum likelihood methods, incorporating data from the originally published wide binary star sample along with their movement across the sky and considering possible errors in distance measurements, yields results consistent with Newton's gravity law and excludes its deviation by a factor of around 5. To achieve a definitive confirmation of or contradiction to the fifth power of gravity law, utilizing wide binary star star systems will demand more precise data, particularly regarding distance measurements.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics.
The solution also highlights the significant difference in wave energy preservation
at large radii between head and tail shocks, with our derived relation h(t) ~
R^(1/2)(dPhi/dt) offering a valuable tool for analyzing shock dynamics near the
star.
The condition for matter ejection is also redefined in terms of specific internal
energy at both large radii and the surface.
The framework is also applicable to infinitely long tubes and yields novel
insights into shock evolution, potentially related to X-ray burst observations.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide a modern and straightforward introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic knowledge of representation theory, and to address a few specific problems relevant to combinatorial representation theory.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper examines the impact of reference data diversity on the conversational model's output, revealing an inverse relationship between the data diversity and the model's generated responses. These findings provide a new direction for developing more innovative conversational models through the use of diverse reference data.

Automated driving systems depend on predictive capabilities to avoid accidents,
however, their reliability varies in various situations, including hazardous maneuvers by other road users.
A specific classification system called RiskAlert uses hazardous change of direction patterns and can
improve the safety of automated driving systems through accurate classifications.
This study explores the application of deep learning methods, specifically convolutional neural networks,
to analyze and predict changes of direction.
Various deep learning models were trained and evaluated based on change of direction speed and trajectory data.
The experiment results demonstrate that a simplified neural network model achieved the best outcome,
correctly classifying 79% of changing directions as either safe or hazardous.
Additionally, the study suggests potential improvements by incorporating real-world driving scenarios into
synthetic scenarios to better prepare the model for actual road conditions.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating phase space and explain how neural networks can be employed 
to model these instrumental effects more comprehensively.  Furthermore, I will 
examine specific examples of applications of this method in the context of $B^0_{s} \to B^0_{s}\bar{B}^0_{s}$ 
decoherence studies and multi-resonance $B^0 \bar{B}^0$ beam spin asymmetry 
measurements.  Initial results from these analyses will also be presented.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, even when dealing with significantly unbalanced datasets. Our research shows that the effectiveness of these methods can be compromised when the dataset distribution is uneven, an issue that often goes unnoticed due to the initial high accuracy achieved on balanced testing data. This shortcoming becomes more apparent over time as the model's performance declines during the incremental learning process. To address this problem, we developed a novel metric called the Bound for Unbalanced Data (BUBD), designed to identify the potential performance degradation beforehand. By establishing an upper limit on accuracy, our evaluation on the ARROWS dataset confirms that traditional learning algorithms tend to exceed this bound, validating our findings.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to address the performance and stability needs during the single support phase. The key benefit of our approach is the minimal complexity added to supervisory controllers, a feature that is crucial for addressing practical applications. The proposed system has been successfully demonstrated with both simulated and real-world robot experiments.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates side-channel-based vulnerabilities into hardware.  To achieve this, a new method of side-channel-based performance degradation, based on simultaneous multithreading architectures, has been examined.  By employing the thread prioritization mechanism, HyperDegrade can force the attack thread to displace higher precedence input threads, thereby increasing the technique's efficacy.  Furthermore, a new algorithm, introduced to minimize overhead while achieving performance degradation, enables HyperDegrade to balance security and performance.  When evaluated on three diverse processors, HyperDegrade exhibits practical feasibility, allowing the attack thread to degrade input threads' energy and energy consumption derivatives without compromising overall system performance.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

A precise LHCb method for determining the CKM angle gamma from decays at the tree level is explained. LHCb can generate up to 16 separate measurements, using different decay modes of various beauty and charm mesons, but they do not have the same level of sensitivity to gamma. By combining all available results, a highly accurate determination is achieved. This paper provides a detailed look at several of these measurements and gives a up-to-date result of $45.0^{+2.3_{stat}}^{+1.6_{syst}}-_{-1.6}^{-1.3}$ degrees, which is consistent with previous results but has a slightly different central value due to different systematic evaluations.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, and it compares this measure with conventional unknotting distances. The study also presents an example to show that the distance measure originating from the diagonal move is not monotonic.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his approach, we derive our cocycle, X, through a differing means, enabling us to establish the resulting invariant's exact order. Additionally, for any given 1-cycle, F within the homology of the space of long knots, we prove the conjunction of the invariant, obtained by integrating I(X) with F, shares the same behavior as the Casson invariant, specifically, it is cohomologous to the canonical generator of H^1(O(3)/GL(2,R)). As an extension of our primary proof, we also examine the scenario of straight-line paths in the space of unknotted spheres embedded in three-dimensional Euclidean space.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider sterile neutrinos, establishing a minimum mass for a single such neutrino flavour.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate and share information, FL can be categorized into different types: traditional, horizontal, or vertical FL. Here, we concentrate on the challenges of vertical FL and a privacy-preserving method to tackle them. In a vertical FL setting, participants who share the same data IDs but have different features can collaborate to train a machine learning model without exchanging their features. A secure multi-party computation protocol is used to ensure privacy during FL by training data samples sequentially. As an alternative to existing encryption methods, we propose using Fully Homomorphic Security Agency to protect data privacy. A proposed FL framework includes steps for FL initialization, a secure vertical training algorithm, and a decision step. Here, a prediction algorithm called Random Forest is employed.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions.

Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart function and is largely dictated by IQC growth rate. However, IQC growth is just one element that dictates intervention timing. Instead, we suggest that patient decision-making is driven by desire, fear, and understanding. These factors are grouped into three categories: desire to delay surgery, fear of sudden right heart failure combined with improved survival rates and non-inclusive Sudden Death Protocols, and understanding involving patient education and involvement. By incorporating these aspects, we aim to create a comprehensive model that considers patient feelings and involvement in decision-making. This model is tested using data from three case studies involving pulmonary valve replacement surgery.

This study explores the long-term properties of phase-field functionals that incorporate slight variations within both their bulk and surface components. The considered functionals embody a specific type of static model that quantifies damage in heterogeneous materials. The model's ultimate behavior is comprehensively defined by Gamma-convergence based on the relative rates at which its approximations and oscillation parameters converge.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster mobile data networks while also providing wireless charging for devices. In this system, communication signals use narrowband modulation techniques, allowing for high-energy harvesting due to high signal efficiency. However, this efficiency comes at the cost of reduced data transmission rates. To balance these concerns, a multi-user model was developed which utilizes broadband modulations for high data transmission rates in a cluster of users, and combines this with narrowband modulations for maximum energy harvesting. The model aims to maximize energy harvesting in a specific time period, given a certain data transmission rate requirement, given the complexity and costs associated with energy harvesting circuits. To solve this problem, an iterative algorithm was developed which harvests energy in two stages: a coarse phase to quickly gain a substantial amount of energy, and a precise phase to fine-tune data transmission rates and energy harvesting. The algorithm distributes energy harvested from narrowband modulations among all users for a fair and equitable charging system. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in achieving an optimal balance between energy harvesting and data transmission rates.

Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

Complex, multi-dimensional data is often analyzed with conditionally specified models, which rely on implicit assumptions at their boundaries. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. The method is then demonstrated with a widely used model, and an alternative condition is also introduced to address limitations in the original Heffernan-Tawn model, particularly regarding its inability to capture certain cases of asymptotic independence.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build upon and improve previous work, particularly Huang et al's. GlossBERT model, which addresses WSD (Huang et al.,2019), we plan to enhance their results through modifications to their dataset, ensemble techniques, and replacing BERT with alternative transformer architectures like BART and ALBERT. A corresponding GitHub repository contains our code, which expands upon the original implementation provided by Huang et al.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often use stochastic diffusion models to assess network vulnerability. However, these models can be computationally expensive and rely on complex simulations. In this study, we present a straightforward approach based on matrix operations that accurately models the spreading process using the Infectious Susceptible (IS) framework. Our method provides precise calculation of the exact and approximate critical thresholds for network breakdown. For the IS model, we derive closed-form equations and an efficient algorithm to determine the critical threshold. For other models, we propose a simple approach to calculate the critical threshold. Like the giant component threshold, our metric is obtained based on node removal strategies and does not require complex simulations. Our results for random networks show high agreement with simulated data.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an optical ring. By analyzing this design in detail using a comprehensive system model and simulated time-domain responses to gravitational waves, we found that the sloshing Sagnac topology effectively bypasses the traditional opto-mechanical feedback control loop stability issue. Furthermore, assuming the use of high-quality optical components, we demonstrated that this design enables stable optical cavity lengths while sensor and actuator fields remain located within the same photodetector mode, thus preventing further feedback. Consequently, this design allows for the optimization of the detector's response function, leading to a significant improvement in high-frequency sensitivity.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to the creation of small solid particles, and ultimately, planetesimals. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in protoplanetary disks. It highlights the distribution of small solid particles, formed through the vertical shear instability, and suggests that their characteristics align with features observed in recent sub-mm/mm wavelength observations. It also predicts findings that future observations with higher sensitivity and resolution will uncover with the aid of advanced telescopes like ALMA and a Next Generation Very Large Array.

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing Wannier functions in the model. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, results show that this assumption leads to inaccuracies. For instance, it erroneously predicts isolated Mn sites and fails to reproduce the correct dispersion and symmetry in XPS spectra. Only by expanding the model to include all relevant orbitals on the O sites does it yield results consistent with experimental data and simple chemical intuition. This study serves as an example of the importance of carefully constructing models and using ab initia methods to inform the construction, particularly in complex materials with significant structural similarities that can confuse simpler models.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of more accurate, detailed models that capture the underlying structure of the material. From these, we identified the smallest models that are stable and consistent with experimental data; two of these models can also be applied to similar materials. These discoveries open up possibilities for using computational modeling to design more effective materials. Additionally, we've determined that certain characteristics in barium titanate, such as the movement of certain atoms and the vibration of the molecular structure, can be controlled through changes to the volume of the material, and further that these changes are influenced by the presence of certain other atoms.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. To investigate and generate new physics at Dirac points, researchers must either substitute carbon with an element having a different valence, employ heavy metals in graphene-like structures, or exploit massive optical or X-ray resonances to induce effective strong interactions. We investigate the latter method and demonstrate how incorporating graphene with intense light fields from external sources can drive Dirac electrons into a massive insulating state. In this setup, graphene interacts with two intense light fields via optical cavities or waveguides. The pumped photons interact with Dirac electrons, effectively making it possible for them to enter a massive insulating phase. The electrons' interaction with the photons can be described as a trilinear coupling, reminiscent of the $\phi^{3}$ theory, and we show that this model yields stable solutions for both optical insulators. The stability of these solutions is short-lived due to decay processes that dissipate the insulating state's energy. To extend their lifetime, it is necessary to minimize the valence of graphene by using ionic liquid gating. The energy and lifetime of these optically-induced insulating states can be described qualitatively using a polaron-like model, and we demonstrate the approach both conceptually and quantitatively.

The unit interval data best fit the beta model; however, the standard beta distribution falls short when dealing with bimodal unit interval data. A novel, bimodal beta distribution is presented, based on an approach utilizing the alpha-skew-normal model. We examine key characteristics of this distribution, including bimodality, real moments, entropy measures, and its unique identifiability. A regression model is also proposed, based on this new distribution, along with a discussion of residual properties. Estimation is achieved via maximum likelihood, supported by a Monte Carlo simulation evaluating the efficacy of these estimators in finite samples, along with a discussion of the outcomes. A real-world application illustrates the proposed distribution's aptitude in modeling data sets with bimodal patterns.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit.

In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer.

This work extends the research of Fittouhi and Joseph in Weierstrass Sections for Parabolic Adjoint Action in Type $A$. Considering an irreducible simple algebraic group $G$ and a Borel subgroup $B$, let's analyze a subgroup $P$ that contains $B$. Further, let's derive the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $P$, denoted by $\mathfrak m$. Research questions concerning the orbits of $B$ acting on $\mathfrak m$ are explored. A specific set of elements within $\mathfrak m$, called weierstrass sections and denoted by $\Sigma$, is also proposed.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional neural training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods.

We investigate the concurrent loss of spatial translation and dilation symmetries in a class of models inspired by the Ginzburg-Landau theory, in which the mechanisms responsible for symmetry breaking are represented by a potential function describing spatial gradients. Our research reveals the existence of modes with subdimensional or zero propagation, characterized as "fractons", where their motion is constrained. The effective field theories of this type encompass systems like helical superfluids and metafluids, in which fractons can be linked to an underlying symmetry associated with higher order charges, resulting in the simplification of some elastic properties. Introducing a finite charge density influences the fracton's mobility, leading to a trade-off between the chemical potential and superfluid velocity in determining the gap of the dilaton. The mobility of fractons can also be modified at zero density by incorporating higher derivative terms.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. These predictions align with forecasts from LISA and other gravitational wave detectors, with a significant PBH population contributing to the gravitational wave signal detectable by LISA at a SNR of 0.15.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture for speech enhancement. The proposed model innovatively incorporates a comprehensive attention mechanism within a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence framework, leveraging previously unexplored information within each individual frame. This innovative approach is an evolution of previous attention-based models. The newly designed bidirectional attention-based sequence-to-sequence model, by integrating bidirectional attention modules, leverages more context within each individual frame. Our proposed bidirectional attention-based sequence-to-sequence model, by incorporating bidirectional attention modules, is capable of leveraging more contextual information within each individual frame. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals keeps air at a slightly lower pressure relative to surrounding areas. This measure prevents potentially harmful contaminated air from leaking out into neighboring spaces. Although the rooms use special filters to treat the released air, even filtered air can contain small particles with biological hazards, thus posing risks to patients, medical staff, and other neighbors. To ensure the effective containment of these rooms we need to design them carefully considering various factors such as the characteristics of the room itself, any possible breaches in the room structure, and both internal and external air currents. Because modeling complex geometries like rooms with equipment can be computationally demanding we instead model the air within the room as being uniformly distributed while considering local high-pressure zones near the air-exit fans. Using this approach we are able to predict key parameters such as the concentration of contaminants both within the room and in the air being expelled.
