However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of our metric function, which optimizes the chances of selecting correct paths during decoding.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model extends the aνMSM framework. In this new model, the axion decay constant is elevated to 10^9 GeV, potentially solving the isocurvature problem while also addressing the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe through leptogenesis in the neutrino sector. With this setup, the right-handed neutrinos can decay into a dark matter component, known as the fuzzy dark matter, consisting of particles with very low mass. Alternatively, dark matter can be produced through scattering interactions with hadrons or through interactions with electroweak bosons or top quarks. This research explores these various production mechanisms and establishes constraints on the model's parameters from observations and experiments.

Between October 2016 and April 2017, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using its new high-resolution spectroscopic instruments. In total, 14 high-resolution spectra were collected as part of the HROS survey. With a focus on 2D spectra, a sample of 1,000 spectra selected from the raw data was analyzed where 84% of the spectra had a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 in less than 3 hours of integration time. It was found that most HROS spectra show three main advantages including improved signal-to-noise ratio, better wavelength calibration and higher resolution compared to the original instrument. However, some issues such as a lower resolution at the short wavelength region and a few pixels with incorrect values were also highlighted. Several methods for correcting these issues were suggested. In an assessment of object classification performance, it was discovered that the training models based on the MAESTRO database could effectively classify objects using the HROS spectra with an accuracy of around 85-87%. It was indicated that with more data collected and a refined training model, better classification performance could be achieved. The HROS spectra possess higher quality that might allow the improvement of several scientific areas including object classification and parameter estimation. The efficient data processing method designed for the HROS data includes a several steps including bias and flat field correction, order extraction, order merging, extraction of 1-dimensional spectra and flux calibration. As

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. This is evident even in more advanced models, where Bilevel Convolutional Network's performance exemplifies both robust texture extraction and precise edge extraction. The BCN model achieves this form of efficiency by incorporating two key components: sparse1x1 convolution and a Relevance Extension Module. The former promotes efficient feature usage, while the latter facilitates effective cross-channel and spatial interactions. As a result, we observe that edge information plays a pivotal role in subsequent stages of feature extraction, particularly in early layers. The BCN model's form of efficiency enables the use of smaller network components, reducing overall size without compromising performance. This is validated through multiple imaging tasks, demonstrating enhanced efficiency and comparable performance to other models. The BCN model's form of efficiency, combined with its unique design, makes it an excellent basis for benchmarking CNN models with forms of efficiency, providing a valuable reference for future research in this domain.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In this paper, we clarify the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verify that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. The our verifications demonstrate that MongoDB provides strong atomicity and consistency in sharded cluster transactions, and that the other deployments also provide a strong version of snapshot isolation.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1988). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored (Stump (2016)).

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right as the probe approached and moved away from its closest point to the sun. These approaches happened between November 2018 and January 2020. To get a better understanding of energy availability for different solar plasma processes, we determined how much energy the solar wind carries over time, normalized to a distance of one solar radius. This allowed us to compare our findings with another space mission, SOHO, which observed the solar wind for a longer period but in a different direction. Our analysis revealed that, on average, the solar wind energy flux values were about 1000 times greater during these close encounters than before, and this increase followed a predictable pattern based on distance from the sun. However, there was a wide variation in these energy flux values, with a difference of nearly ten thousand times between the lowest and highest values, which indicated that the solar wind energy behaves in an unpredictable manner and might challenge the assumptions of different models. Although these data exclude certain regions and boundaries, they offer valuable insights for scientists studying processes within and before the solar wind.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance increases of 9% and 14% in real-time scenarios.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.

Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressureless voids form behind the shock front, and even at higher indices, these empty spaces do not expand infinitely, and solution profiles remain largely similar. However, a key difference emerges as the adiabatic index approaches 4/3, showing up both in an approximate and exact form.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to extract key parameters for both models.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within an asymmetrical SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in tidal features as galaxy mass increased. Additionally, we established relations between tidal features and stellar mass in these massive early-type galaxies. Specifically, we found that about 50 percent of tidal features were too insignificant to detect and that their formation was influenced by a stochastic process. The features observed also displayed no preference in rotation direction and were more common around galaxies with intermediate galaxy concentrations. Our findings imply tidal features can act as a useful tool in studying galaxy interactions and mergers based on their merger rate exceeding that required to match the observed features around massive early-type galaxies in this depth survey.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates resources to current students based on the needs of both existing and future generations. Our model shows that investing in higher education can increase the social mobility of future generations at the expense of present resources. Under certain conditions, a social planner would prioritize long-term benefits over immediate ones. Furthermore, the presence of a education investment can alter the intergenerational social mobility structure, particularly in societies with significant mobility restrictions.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the maximum absolute value of the functions does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $2000 \log^5 n \cdot K^{2p} \varepsilon^{-2} \log (n/\varepsilon)^{3000 \log^5 n \cdot K^{2p} \varepsilon^{-2}}$ and for all $j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $k \in \{0,1\}$, the $\ell_p$ norm of $x_j$ raised to the power of $p/2$ is within $\varepsilon$ of the $\ell_p$ norm of $v_j$, and this relationship holds for the linear functional $x_j(t) + k$ as well, and this relationship holds for $x_j(t) - k$ as well and this relationship holds for $x_j(t) + k$ as well and

At the Large Hadron Collider, so-called "emittance scans" are conducted to determine the precision with which the distance between interaction points can be measured as a function of filled betatron oscillation modes. These "scans" actually refer to carefully planned runs at specific energy levels where the characteristics of the particle beams are manually adjusted to interact more effectively with the detection luminosity. This document accurately describes the particle beam characteristics at various runs during the LHC's Run 1, especially near its maximum energy level, and also outlines the interaction physics yields predicted by the LHC's theoretical models (PYTHIA 6.4 and GEANT3) for actual lhc2009-pS2-data-level-trig-nubars-inclusive-p020.pbzd.dat.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints on solution accuracy. A numerical example is also included to illustrate the theoretical findings.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in communication/computation energy consumption and BS switching, while also promoting energy-saving modes in BSs.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain information, we can accurately assess various pressures without being hindered by natural linewidth limitations. In experiments conducting up to eight simultaneous pressure broadening measurements across three O2/N2 probe pairs, we can accurately derive real-time pressure information using a customized least-squares algorithm. As a result, we can gather precise 3D data sets of temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios over large volumes, even in highly turbulent and dynamically changing flows.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that there is a break that interacts with both charged and neutral modes. The results demonstrate that neutral modes can carry information, and this concept is further explored through an application that recovers a dc current even when source and bias are at equilibrium. This is possible due to statistical correlations between electron states, and it is shown that these correlations can be utilized to generate a dc current from noise currents in the edge. The factor that determines this is not affected by the question of whether quantum mechanics is fundamental. Additionally, it is demonstrated that both effect can be observed using photoluminescence, and an experimental demonstration is proposed.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices.

We have examined the hard-disk model from a thermodynamic perspective, breaking down pressure as a function of density for various temperatures and vice versa. Our analysis reveals distinct behavioral regimes in the hard-disk system, characterized by unique, smooth, or abrupt changes, and we have located the precise location of a second-order phase transition. Furthermore, based on recent studies, we propose a new critical point as a possible endpoint for these transitions. By simulating the system's mean potential energy and clustering information, we have identified the location of the endpoint. Our findings suggest that the endpoint lies at a specific point, and we have confirmed this through direct comparison with previously estimated values.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared data from the WISE survey. We calculated the reduction in cluster brightness caused by interstellar dust and found it to vary between 1.54 and 3.22 in reddening and 2.15 and 4.35 in extinction. Three of these candidates showed a concentration of stars within a small angular area, yet further analysis revealed them to be either distant objects, collapsing star groups, or even future supergiant stars. We also estimated their ages and chemical compositions, as well as the rate at which they are rotating on their axes. Our research highlights the importance of observing the galaxy's bulge for longer and with more precision to fully understand its globular cluster population.

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal{T}_1$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions at scale $q_T$ alongside mass corrections to the partonic invariant mass $M$ function. Our study provides N$^3$LL resummation of large logarithms in massless limit and explores the impact of finite quark-mass corrections at both massless and heavy-quark dominant scale relationships, demonstrating that massless resummation may overestimate large logarithms when considering the mass-dependent beam and $M$ functions. As a result, exclusive differential spectra can offer valuable insights for understanding the nature

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. The investigation employs linear response theory to calculate the effects of light on these materials, utilizing the Kubo formula. The results show that the velocity-based approach accurately represents light-matter interactions, whereas the dipole-based approach can be misleading due to possible ambiguities arising from the gauge transformation. These findings suggest that the long-standing preference for the velocity-based approach is supported, as using the dipole-based approach may yield erroneous, gauge-dependent outcomes.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the requirement of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. By conducting comprehensive
experiments and experiments with simulated noise, we discover that the
Original CNN model exhibits the most consistent and accurate predictive capabilities
across multiple process datasets and can also handle real-world data, predicting
accurate process-event occurrence times with up to 10-minute precision.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to be informed about the earthquake's impact and the availability of assistance. A comparative study of sentiment and topic issues before and after the earthquake, as well as a field study, validated our findings. Our open-source code is available for replication on GitHub.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed with high precision, which provides the capability to assess exoplanet biosignatures by evaluating active M-dwarfs. As a result, studying these flares is essential to identify potential targets for more in-depth analysis using upcoming space telescopes. In this study, we present observations of four active M-dwarfs that exhibited exceptional variability during a period of observation, which were chosen because they had favorable conditions for habitability and could be studied with space telescopes in the coming decade. Through a high-resolution space-based spectrometer, we aim to study the chemical composition and physical properties of these flares. So far, we have been able to simulate and schedule a portion of this research using the 6.5-m MMT telescope, which has been approved for funding through the NSF. As such, this research will be possible to execute with the James Webb Space Telescope, the Large Aquarius Observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Extremely Large Telescope. Therefore, it is crucial for the MMT to be available to study these flares before, during, and after the launch of these space-based observatories. As such, this research will be a critical step in our understanding of exoplanet biosignatures and the potential for life beyond our own solar system.

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models to derive exact equations describing wave propagation in a finite number of connected units. Analyzing this through generalized parametric space, researchers discovered that when PT symmetry breaks, propagating modes appear consistently, unaffected by the unit cell's transmission phase or number. However, at PT-symmetric equilibrium, mode formation relies on the unit cell's transmission phase. Notably, reflectionless and perfectly transmissible states can be achieved by selecting specific PT phases and numbers of connected units. Two methods were identified to induce CPAL - operating an odd-numbered series of units at a specific point or using a particular broken phase in conjunction with an allotropic transmission phase in multiple units. This research provides theoretical groundwork for PT-symmetric photonics, enabling a deeper understanding and control of extraordinary light phenomena.

We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult for the network to reach a stable state. Despite this challenge, we are able to extend the method to capture these long-range effects, and as a result, we obtain more accurate predictions of how the network evolves over time.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations. To facilitate their robustness against such tricks, it's crucial to first understand the types of transformations that should be considered safe and accepted in the point cloud context. A systematic analysis has been conducted to identify common transformations used in point cloud research, resulting in three main categories: basic transformations (such as rotation and translation), complex transformations (such as deformation and scaling), and environment-transformations involving adding the point cloud to various surfaces or modifying the surrounding surroundings. Additionally, a dataset named EnvType has been introduced to classify environmental transformations including objects and surroundings in the scene. Furthermore, a dataset called DeformType has been created to depict various deformation types in traffic signs. These resources can assist researchers in experimenting with realistic and context-relevant transformations for improving the robustness of training in the point cloud context.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, where the classic ALOHA protocol is being re-examined in the context of these radar networks due to its simplicity and exam readiness, and we're also comprehending and evaluating the clear channel assessment, or CCA, which is employed in the widely adopted CSMA protocols and frequently leads to unnecessary delays. To evaluate our modifications, we've developed analytical models in the form of closed-form equations that excel at providing initial results and are easy to implement, although they may not provide the most precise outcomes when multi-valued functions are involved, and as an alternative we've carried out simulations to obtain the most accurate results, and we've found that the initial equations are capable of providing the most reliable results under typical conditions, and we've also determined that the default CSMA CCA process introduces unneeded delays that can be eliminated by either skipping it entirely or by implementing a more exam-ready procedure that can be thoroughly tested and compared against the current implementation and found to provide the most exam-ready results.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient training through non-saturating penalty terms but also enable the use of a custom loss function to enhance textual coherence. Experimental evaluations on multiple text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance and coherent output compared to current state-of-the-art models.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions are used to constrain cosmological parameters from mock HI cosmology and catalog data. In collaboration with researchers at the University of Texas at Austin, we conduct a comparative analysis of first- and second-order contributions to the bisine spectrum for the SIMPLIFY survey, a simulated HI intensity mapping survey with 6 GHz bandwidth and $1 nK^2$ temperature noise. Comparing these theoretical predictions with previous models and catalog simulations, we constrain several key cosmological parameters, including HI bias, B-mode orientation, neutrino mass, fR4, and the linear and nonlinear growth factors. Notably, we find that the B-mode signal can be used to determine the orientation of the sky map with an accuracy of up to 5 degrees. Additionally, by combining multiple constraints, we are able to constrain the nonlinear growth factor within 6%. The methods and findings presented here will inform the data analysis and scientific insights of upcoming HI intensity mapping surveys, such as those planned for the Array of Aperture Antennas and the Precise HI survey.

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling simultaneous estimation of population density, standard SCR model parameters, and resource selection behavior even in the absence of telemetry data.  Our method offers a flexible approach that can be applied to diverse study designs commonly found in capture-recapture and spatial modeling contexts.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking.

Dissipative systems exhibit varied behavior in response to external inputs or initial disturbances, with some networks localizing dynamic processes and others spreading them. This study derives a precise expression for nodal activity that can be used to classify complex networks. Furthermore, a general formula is proposed that assesses the localizing or spreading nature of specific nodes within different types of networks, including those with central hubs. This framework is applied to understand complex systems such as power grids and neuroscience networks.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of critical data during games. Previous researchers developed models for assessing football teams' defensive skills by relying on available tracking data, but they focused primarily on player movement and neglected the influence of goal-scoring opportunities. To address this limitation, we developed a comprehensive hierarchical model aiming to evaluate the contribution of individual players to goal prevention in football. Our approach involves linking team and individual defensive performance to goal-conversion opportunities through an process-oriented model, incorporating player movement as an influential factor rather than a direct one. By adopting this model, we were able to examine the performance of the English Premier League 2018-19 season and discovered that teams with higher press intensity actually lead to more goal-scoring chances, contrary to conventional assumptions.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of C and X in terms of exact sequences. This leads to finding subvarieties within the Jacobian of X that are isogenous to the Jacobian of D, by detecting points in the Theta-divisor of X that have rational values under a specific map to the Jacobian of D.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified single-layer representations.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a tool for the automated generation, assessment, and further development of reliable software. This environment features the testing tools' interconnectedness with formal verification and formal methods tools. This document details the architecture of a prototype system and discusses the principles underlying geometric testing. The case studies presented illustrate the application of these principles in the context of a diverse range of problems, including the testing of math proofs, program analyses, and machine learning models.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field applied to the spin. This property makes the system ideal for demonstrating the coexistence of two kinds of photon bundle emissions, with one type emitting 2$m$-correlated photons and the other 2$n$-correlated photons, with $m \neq n$.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate for a large majority of nodes (at least a fraction 1 - O(delta)) with an extremely large network (at least an exponentially growing function of 1/delta).
