The algorithm operates with a polynomial amount of time, communication, and processing per node, and it requires only a very small number of nodes to be 'honest' (at least a fraction 2/3 + O(delta)) of the total network. Our algorithm combines techniques such as random sampling through 'balls and bins' mechanisms and efficient size estimation within hierarchical trees.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed method's accuracy
rivals or surpasses alternative methods with little to no loss in accuracy,
depending on the traffic flow relative to the intersection's capacity.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and Seebeck coefficient. The anomalous Nernst effect in these films is strongly temperature dependent, with the anomalous Nernst coefficient exhibiting values up to 50 $\mu$V/K/K at room temperature, significantly larger than the magnetic Seebeck effect.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into experiments. By leveraging both machine learning and synchrotron light sources at user facilities, researchers can accelerate materials characterization even further.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from one to the other allows for finding a near-ground-state configuration. In cases where energy level crossings occur, quantum measurements may yield excited states instead of the desired ground state. To avoid this issue, the "quantum adiabatic theorem" suggests slowly diagonalizing the Hamiltonian during the transition. However, achieving this goal is complicated due to the exponential growth of Hilbert space dimensions. To address this challenge, the "quantum adiabatic algorithm" was created to find an efficient way to navigate these vast spaces by localizing wave functions and applying a tailored change of basis that limits calculations to relevant subspace configurations. As a result, the driver Hamiltonian can be simplified to a basic form, significantly reducing the number of variables required to represent the wave functions. This simplification has a direct impact on the choice of quantum annealing protocols, which must account for non-exponential growth in both space and operator sizes. These findings have important implications for understanding and executing successful quantum adiabatic computations.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957 are examined.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of space is considered, denoted as the 'large volume regime.' This achievement comes from a deeper examination of a specific surface-related problem that includes an unknown boundary, both within the confined object and at an infinitely distant point. The analysis involves the discovery of a specific term in an equation, termed 'isoperimetric residue,' which helps in expanding an isoperimetric problem equation when the 'large volume regime' is approached. A key component of the study on these'residues' is a newly introduced flatness standard for surface types that have a limited average curvature and can be used to better understand minimal surface types that have unique points.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components. This model is based on streaming data from ongoing experiments. The algorithm uses a method to predict all the possible system outcomes and establish a theoretical limit on its performance when the actual dynamics are known. The study shows that providing the algorithm with more side information or trial data results in tighter performance guarantees. The algorithm's effectiveness is confirmed by simulations on advanced flight simulator and other complex dynamical systems that are hard to model.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that couples to a particular lepton in a way that leads to a unusually persistent production and significant travel distance before decay.  The model's scalar field exhibits a distinctive "turn-off" mechanism that leads to a larger interaction cross-section near matter's density and an even more extraordinary effect that reduces the cross-section by many orders of magnitude near the matter's core.  The theoretical model's framework is validated by existing experimental evidence and the proposed near-Earth behavior of the model is also examined.  The theoretical model's framework is also used to reevaluate the micro-black hole production and detection possibility at the LHC and future colliders, and the proposed detection criteria are also examined in the context of micro-black hole's interaction with the detector and decay products' energy distribution.  The findings suggest that micro-black hole detection is unlikely due to its characteristic size and interaction length with matter, which leads to its nearly complete evaporation inside the detector.  The theoretical model's framework is also compared to other BSM scenarios involving micro-black holes and dark photons.  The results suggest that a specific class of non-gravitational micro-black hole models may be evolutionarily stable if they remain neutral in charge.  The findings also indicate that dark photons can exist near Earth if they remain associated with charged, heavy objects.  The micro-black hole's characteristic size and interaction length with matter are found to be outside the expected detection range at the LHC and future colliders,

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning platforms in the fall of 2020 and 2021. The study analyzed logon frequency, assignment submission rates, and exam scores, data was divided into two cohorts and further categorized by first-generation university student status, ethnic minority status, and gender. The results indicated that students who were the first in their family to attend university or belonged to ethnic minority groups were more likely to fall behind during the first cohort's remote learning period. In contrast, gender did not show any significant influence on submission frequencies or exam scores. To catch up with peers during the first cohort's remote learning, an additional 18 percent of class time was needed. However, this was reduced to just 10 percent in the second cohort, suggesting that falling behind was less pronounced in the second cohort. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic differences when assessing learning outcomes during remote learning and suggest that the 2020 pandemic restrictions on university campus access may have contributed to unequal learning outcomes.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a non-extremal black hole, transforming its singularity from a cold, isolated singularity into a hot singularity with infinite temperature.

In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over an extended period of 6 hours of continuous walking. This indicates a high potential for using extended BCI systems to restore independent mobility impaired individuals who were previously unable to walk.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, mating, avoiding predators, adapting to environmental changes, and maintaining social interactions. The ability of animals to engage in complex behaviors depends on their capacity to move efficiently through their surroundings. Understanding the underlying mechanisms that enable animals to navigate their environments is a fundamental question that has significant implications across multiple disciplines. This review aims to provide an interdisciplinary framework that explores the mechanisms behind animal navigation, emphasizing the interconnected nature of sensory inputs, neural processing, and resulting movements. Furthermore, this framework will be used to examine the unique characteristics of the locomotor system that have evolved to support diverse locomotor behaviors and will also highlight opportunities for further research and the potential applications of these findings in multiple fields.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, through an effective approach, separately for the light and heavy Higgs components. The analysis includes the impact of finite loops comprising the top, charm, and bottom quarks. A through examination of the dependence on the phase of the Higgs mixing angle is conducted. The resulting implications for the search for CP-odd Higgs bosons at the LHC are explored. The analysis of the $\pp \to h_b$ process is also conducted through a thorough, leading-order calculation separately for the complex scalar and pseudoscalar components, with the effects of SUSY corrections and a through discussion of SUSY particle phase dependencies.

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance.

Declarative networks are a novel framework that enables the direct differentiation of the solution mappings resulting from optimizing a parameterized problem. This approach allows us to model complex systems and their behaviors without delving into specific implementations, simply by examining their overall properties. As long as certain mathematical conditions are met, we can derive explicit formulas describing these network behaviors and, crucially, differentiate them with ease. This capability holds significant potential for optimizing complex systems across various disciplines, given the widespread applicability of optimization principles and the limitations imposed by traditional iterative methods.

A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes.

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by laser beams. The approach is monitored for quantum jumps that result in the transfer of a photon from one cavity to the other. The precision of the measurement can be increased beyond the standard limit by taking advantage of quantum feedback and the phenomenon known as measurement-induced superposition. The approach is also robust against imprecise knowledge of the system and its environment. The role of the quantum feedback control is further examined, and the conditions are studied that lead to measurement-induced collapse and the phenomenon known as Zeno dynamics. The approach is compared to the method utilizing GHZ states, and the results show that the proposed method offers greater stability and can surpass 50,000 times the precision achieved with the results induced by the GHZ-state.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2005 to 2018. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

This paper explores the behavior of Smarandache's sequence from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) at A061076, specifically focusing on its associated sequences, A061077 and A061078, linked to the Smarandache's sigma product of digits. We address open questions by identifying upper bounds applicable to all natural numbers 'n', as well as deriving closed formulas for sequences 'a(n)' and 'b(n)'. Our combined results provide insights into the behavior of the broader sequence 'c(n)'. To validate our findings, accompanying examples using Wolfram Mathematica scripts are included.

Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a larger scale.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and HPC systems, revealing that system noise and variability can substantially impact both performance and cost at both small and large scales.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the effective use of these frameworks also relies on the well-being of employees working from home. Studies suggest that implementing Scrum can have both positive and negative effects on employee well-being. With the rapid adoption of remote working in recent years, there is a pressing need to better understand the impact of this new working environment on individuals. As a self-determination theory-based measure is used to assess employee needs, our study aims to identify which psychological requirements are crucial for supporting well-being in this new working environment. By conducting a large-scale online survey and analyzing the data through descriptive statistics, we found that well-being is often compromised in remote working environments, with the following needs being crucial: the desire for competence, the desire for relatedness, and the desire for autonomy. With these findings in hand, we discuss the implications for both theory and practice in line with self-determination theory.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), our research investigates the application of retargeting to improve the efficiency of policy learning. Unlike Kallus (2020), we distinguish between the author's approach and that of retargeting, focusing on differences in the use of data from the testing distribution. Our findings demonstrate that the efficiency gain from retargeting is substantial when the reference distribution is distinct from the testing distribution. Notably, a significant improvement is observed even with a minimal difference, resulting in a substantial reduction in mean squared error. Our research extends Kallus (2020) in two key areas: first, we provide a more comprehensive efficiency gain result that does not assume a specific form for the treatment effect. Secondly, we investigate the efficiency gain resulting from using a different reference distribution, an aspect not explored in Kallus (2020). Our research contributes to the broader field of decision-making under uncertainty, with potential applications in areas such as healthcare, education, and marketing.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a derivative of the Linear Canonical Transform, and proves related inequalities, including Heisenberg's Inequality and a logarithmic inequality for LCST.

This work utilizes the non-grounded user channel model to analyze the extreme values of optimal power control in a network without considering the ground effect. We derive closed-form expressions for the extremal gain of optimal power control, specifically for maximum and minimum configurations. It is shown that the extremal values scale as O(log k) where k represents the number of users. A series of numerical experiments is performed to provide precise gain values for both extremal scenarios. The results provide a basis for evaluating the improvement provided by optimal power control in a network.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being trapped in areas of high velocity, resulting in reduced turbulence and smaller pressure drops, whereas our algorithm that uses a smaller time step for particle collisions correctly demonstrates that turbulence promotes the lifting of particles from bed regions during the upstroke of oscillatory flows. Although our results for fluid and overall mass transport match those obtained using the standard method, our findings reveal that the choice of time step for resolving particle collisions can significantly impact the simulation of particle interactions, potentially leading to incorrect data that is indistinguishable from measured data without further analysis.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1 to 4, studies revealed a corresponding increase in the feedforward control system's performance.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air phase's behavior is further compounded when the vaporized water from the droplet's surface generates an asymmetrical distribution of concentration as the droplet is in motion. The implications of this effect on the droplet's absorption of particles from the surrounding gas phase are an area of ongoing investigation. The challenges that the water vapor concentration effects pose for the efficient collection of particles by the droplet are starting to resemble the obstacles that the droplet itself faces when attempting to repel particles from the surrounding air.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation. Notably, we found a substantial discrepancy between the predictions of prominent models and actual human input, indicating that negation remains a challenging aspect for current English reading comprehension models. CONDAQA serves as a crucial benchmark for assessing the performance of systems processing negated statements in text, systems that should aspire to match human-level performance.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian that result in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench model. Specifically, it is proven that when the system starts in its ground state and undergoes a random quench, the point at which the system Loses coherence marks the minimal gap, however, when the duration of the quench is sufficiently extended, the coherence loss no longer occurs, and instead, characteristic interlacing behavior of energy levels emerges. These findings provide valuable insights into optimizing quantum annealing protocols and have potential implications for understanding and managing information leakage in quantum computers.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbitals, with
doping determined solely by extra electrons. 
Here, a one-band approximation fails and one can instead use a effective
one-band model with an adjusted filling level. 
The starting point for this scenario is quite different from cuprates, with
one instead effective band as opposed to two.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored.

Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors as composed of coupled CuO2 layers. Yet, the cuprates exhibit sufficiently separate layers, rendering these models inappropriate. Our study reveals the presence of long-range Coulomb coupling between the cuprate layers, coupled with electromagnetic flux screening similar to the intralayer coupling. This discovered 'stack' framework, incorporating both short and long-range couplings, directly results in the Gorkov-McMillan BCS theory for layered structures. A notable outcome of the stack model is the formation of the interlayer penetration depth, which has the same relationship to the intralayer penetration depth, as the resistivity has to the normal state resistivity, all by a factor of ~10-4. This proportionality holds true, near the superconducting transition temperature, for multiple samples, including those with tilting and rotating. A 2005 theoretical prediction is confirmed, indicating that the ratio of the interlayer to intralayer penetration depths is directly proportional to the ratio of the cuprate's resistivity to the normal state's resistivity. This explains the previously unanticipated, small ratio of ~10-4 observed in various cuprate samples.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, the sound velocity within it is anticipated to either stabilize at a limiting value or continue rising, ultimately approaching the speed of light. Furthermore, the average sound velocity within the star is essential in linking its radius to its mass. Furthermore, the equation of state's nature significantly impacts the variation of the sound velocity with density, especially when dense matter exhibits quasi-relativistic behavior. Lastly, the interplay between nuclear interactions and dense matter is further explored through the use of stochastic volume terms, which define the energy density's behavior at varying densities.

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. Two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ are mapped anti Tai to each other under weight $w$ if for any corresponding nodes $(u,v)$ with associated weights $(w_u,w_v)$, $u$ being an ancestor of $v$ implies $w_u+w_v\leq w$. Finding the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between two trees turns out to be a computationally easy problem, and we find its optimal solution based on dynamic allocation. Moreover, we show that a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping self is equivalent to a partitioning of a tree into subtree components.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase and amplitude characteristics. Building on previous studies of a specific type that showed promise in estimating parameters, we extend this by investigating another variant of the same state to compare its performance. Through computation of a relevant quantum indicator, we find that this new state outperforms its predecessor in sensitivity, with both states displaying unique features and applications in amplifying weak signals. As a result, these states could be valuable for use in detectors, potentially enhanced through non-demolition measurement processes.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle growth and settling effects. Combining this model with stability criteria for VSI and an equation describing how velocity variations evolve over time, we identify specific conditions under which VSI can be controlled by the development of particles. As it turns out, VSI can be stabilized by particle growth when the growth rate surpasses a certain rate, defined by various factors like shear and thermal diffusion. Similarly, the VSI can be stabilized by particle settling when the settling rate is greater than a specific rate, defined by a critical value of the Grashof number and various other variables. Notably, large-scale VSI is more easily affected by particle growth and settling than smaller-scale VSI, making it essential to consider how the VSI influences particles in a range of sizes. In a finding, we observe that the development and settling of particles have a major effect on VSI in a wide range of distances from being negligible to completely preventing it in certain areas of a specific disk model

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network architecture called the global average pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in fully connected networks. Furthermore, this study confirms that such hidden functionalities are nearly impossible to eradicate once established, thus making them extremely resilient.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assumes absolute motion and relies on a specific theoretical framework known as the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$. Research aims to analyze the impact of $\gamma$-gamma variations on first-generation parametric tests. To achieve this, we conducted simulations based on simulated data, modeling the Earth's and solar system's motion with special relativity. In doing so, we examined how $\gamma$-gamma deviations affect parallax, aberration, and light time variations. Results indicate that $\gamma$'s effect on theoretical tests may be negligible, as post-illon and solar system motion deviations are minimal. However, $\gamma$-gamma impacts first, resulting in theoretical deviations up to 1700 nano-arc-seconds in parallax estimations. These effects are largely unrelated to motion and originate from an infinite-distance shift. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time.

Certain fundamental models that describe one-dimensional two-component Bose-Einstein condensates exhibit exact soliton solutions. However, some of these solutions are topologically non-trivial and therefore unphysical. In this research, we investigate whether there are topologically trivial variants of these solutions and find that certain models do support such non-destructive solitons. Our theoretical predictions are further validated by preparing a Bose-Einstein condensate soliton through a quasi-1D experiment and observing its stable core with a density approximately 50% lower than the surrounding region. This achievement is made possible by utilizing a novel in-situ imaging technique known as paraxial optical tomography.

Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. Also, we discovered three low-luminosity HI galaxies at various distances from M101 that may be associated with its expanding HI disk. The data obtained from the observation of these HI galaxies and their interaction with M101 are consistent with our findings. Additionally, an unequal HI distribution around the galaxy IC 3380 is observed, which is more similar to that of M101. This suggests the possibility of a similar low-luminosity HI galaxy or a passing dwarf galaxy near IC 3380, and future optical observations will be essential to verify this. Our results offer new insights into the presence of hidden HI galaxies around spiral galaxies and have implications for our understanding of how galaxies interact with each other.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can influence local dynamics and potentially signal the cometary environment. To understand this phenomenon, theoretical models incorporating cometary nuclear parameters, plasma plasma parameters, and molecular ion parameters are necessary. As an example, molecular ion parameters for ionized water, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen are analyzed. The resulting spectral models show good agreement with observed cometary spectra, particularly in the 300-450 nm range where water hose and its related molecules have prominent features. Molecular cations play a crucial role in comet nuclei energy balance due to their high ion recombination rates resulting in efficient ultraviolet photons that contribute to the cometary energy balance.

The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

The provided article introduces an Itô-Wentzell type formula tailored to accommodate paths with α-Hölder regularity of $\alpha$ within the interval $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}]$. Additionally, it expands on prior work by R. Castrequini and P. Catuogno concerning Young integrals, as well as research by C. Keller and J. Zhang on rough paths.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This issue becomes even more pronounced when the graph contains a significant number of disconnected subgraphs. To tackle this challenge, we propose an innovative algorithm combining gradient aggregation and multi-step gradient boosting techniques. By adjusting the communication frequency based on distance and incorporating the concept of a mixing time, our algorithm overcomes this issue, requiring only $O\left(\sqrt{\log \left(1/\varepsilon\right)}\right)$ rounds of server-based communications to achieve an $\varepsilon$-accurate probability within each subgraph.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting by modifying data training. The method has particular potential for improving semi-supervised medical image segmentation, a challenging topic due to the high cost of medical image annotation. Our approach is versatile and can also be applied to semi-supervised learning in other fields. As a demonstration, our technique was tested on three medical image segmentation challenges: cell segmentation in endoscopic images, tumor segmentation in dermoscopic images, and polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images. The best results were achieved by adapting data training with our technique, yielding a 2.5% improvement in segmentation accuracy for cell, a 4.7% improvement for tumor, and a 1% improvement for colonoscopy polyps. These results were obtained without using more complex models, simply by enhancing the training data. Our technique's results are striking considering the semi-supervised learning challenges these experiments represent, with often scarce training data.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade known as the High-Luminosity LHC. This upgrade will also involve an overhaul of the LHC's cooling system, resulting in the HL-LHC. The ATLAS upgrade includes enhancements to the calorimeters and coverage of muon systems to improve particle detection. A key component of this upgrade is the ATLAS Trigger and Pre-Trigger system, which has been designed to handle significantly more data and feature upgraded processing units and custom firmware. This system has also received an external evaluation using a dedicated hardware setup, resulting in an external review of its performance characteristics and results of testing ATLAS upgrade features designed for particle detection and muon tracking. This evaluation has also known as the ATLAS Tier-0 facility.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between flexibility and efficiency for flexibly changing
objects.  Extending this concept to the use of skeletal joints, Deferred Neural
Photorealistic Rendering creates a performance--efficient framework for creating
realistic avatars that can be easily adjusted and quick to generate.  Unlike prior
art methods, DNRPR enables the production of photorealistic avatars in real-time
or near real-time while retaining texture details from scan data, even when
invoking changes to the underlying body pose.  This is made possible by utilizing
an inverse compositional technique to pre-calculate how surface transformations
affect image changes, allowing the rendering process to remain efficient and
flexible.  As a result, DNRPR can utilize high-resolution textures and normal maps
directly on the Oculus Rift's RTX rendering pipeline and still deliver a 45 frames
per second performance.  To evaluate its capabilities, we ran several experiments
at various resolution and down-sampling rates.  These tests demonstrated that DNRPR
can effectively preserve fine detail and resist pose-related artifacts, outperforming
both traditional and neural-based rendering methods.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain
